title: Arjuna asks, why act at all?
hookLine: Arjuna catches his teacher in what looks like a contradiction
carry: karma yoga: work offered to god doesn't bind

lines: WHY PUSH ME INTO THIS DEED?
cards: If understanding is better than action, why push me into this terrible deed? That, in paraphrase, is how chapter three of the Gita begins.

In chapter two, Krishna praised a steady understanding and said plain action falls far below it. And all along, he'd been telling Arjuna to stand up and fight. Arjuna is confused, and a little irritated.
Your words seem mixed, he says. Tell me the one thing that's good for me. Now we read these chapters again, slowly, with the old commentators at our elbow.

teach.h: NOBODY STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.
teach.b: Nobody can stay even a moment without acting. Every being is made to act by the forces of its own nature. Sitting still is an act.
Breathing is an act. So the question was never whether to act, but how. Here Krishna brings in an old word: yajna, sacrifice, offering.

teach.h: THE QUESTION IS WHAT KIND OF ACTION.
teach.b: The world is bound by action, he says, except action done as offering. Do your work in that spirit, free of clinging. Then a short creation story.
In the beginning, the Creator brought forth beings together with sacrifice and said: by this you will flourish. You nourish the gods, and the gods will nourish you.

teach.h: ACTION DONE AS OFFERING DOESN'T BIND.
teach.b: Rain, food, work, offering, rain again.

teach.h: THE WHEEL: NOURISH AND BE NOURISHED.
teach.b: Krishna calls it a wheel set turning, and says a person who takes from it and doesn't help turn it lives in vain.
So karma, in chapter three, is first the plain word for action, and only then the web of consequences it sets going.

This is karma yoga, the yoga of action: you can't stop working, so offer the work, and it stops binding you. It's why many Hindus offer food to God before they eat, or quietly offer a day's work before they begin it.
Shankara, glossing sacrifice in this verse, says it means the Lord himself, and quotes an older Vedic line: sacrifice is Vishnu. So for him, action done as offering is action done for God.
Either way, the verse says the same thing about the doer: act, and let go of the grip.

how: Some Hindus begin a day's work, or a meal, by mentally offering it to God, and some Gita study groups read chapter three alongside a classical commentary such as Shankara's.

o: a points system the gods keep on your good deeds
a ritual that only priests are allowed to perform
action, which no one avoids, best done as offering

games.q: Gita, chapter three — tap the pairs.

s: Krishna tells Arjuna he can choose to stop acting altogether
he says no one can stay even a moment without acting.
in chapter three, action done as offering doesn't bind
the world is bound by action, except action done as sacrifice.
Shankara reads the word sacrifice in this verse as the Lord
he quotes the Vedic line that sacrifice is Vishnu.

games.q: Krishna says no one can stay a moment without acting. so what does he tell Arjuna to do?
o: act, and offer the action, so it doesn't bind.
act only when there's something to gain.
games.why: nobody can stop acting, Krishna says, but action done as yajna, an offering, doesn't bind. that's karma yoga.

practice: For the first few breaths, try to do nothing at all, and notice that you can't: the breath goes on, the heart goes on, the body keeps its balance.
Then find one place in an ordinary day where you mostly take from the wheel and give little back, without judging it, and one small way to put something back.
If you pray, you can hold that small return before Krishna, or the one you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Karma. In chapter three, first the plain word for action, which nobody escapes; done as an offering, it becomes karma yoga, and doesn't bind.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: karma, action, the deed done. In Gita chapter three, the plain word for doing.

carryVoice: Your line: karma yoga: work offered to God doesn't bind. Tomorrow, a king who was also a sage. See you then.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.49 (action far inferior to the yoga of understanding)

Bhagavad Gita 3.10–3.16 (the Creator, sacrifice, the wheel)
